Q4501499.summary: Christ gazes out from a gold background, blessing with his right hand and holding a jeweled Gospel book in his left. Painted in hot wax with a vividness close to late Roman portraiture, this is the earliest known surviving icon of Christ as Pantocrator, 'Ruler of All', and one of the most important images in Christian art. Its living, searching face has shaped the Orthodox image of Christ for nearly fifteen centuries.
facts: The two sides of the face differ subtly in eyes, brows and expression, which many interpret as expressing Christ's two natures, divine and human, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon in 451.
Because it had been almost entirely overpainted in the 13th century, it was long thought to date from that period; only in 1962 was it recognized as a mid-6th-century original.

It escaped the destruction of Byzantine Iconoclasm (726–843) because Sinai had passed under Muslim rule in the 640s, placing the remote desert monastery beyond the reach of imperial iconoclast policy.
The panel measures about 84 × 45.5 cm (it was originally larger) and may have been an imperial gift from Justinian, who founded the monastery between 548 and 565.
Q4501499.notes: Production in Constantinople is a widely held inference (possible imperial gift at the monastery's foundation, 548–565), not a documented fact.
